q: An inertial frame of reference is a frame in which:
o: the frame is always accelerating uniformly
Newton's first law holds: a body with no net force keeps a constant velocity
only gravitational forces can act on bodies
the frame rotates at a constant angular speed
x: An inertial frame is one that is not accelerating, so a body with zero net force stays at rest or moves with constant velocity (Newton's first law holds). A rotating frame is tempting because its angular speed is constant, but rotation means acceleration, so it is non-inertial.

q: Which of the following is a non-inertial frame of reference?
o: A car moving along a straight road at a constant 20 m s⁻¹
A train standing at rest at a station
A spaceship drifting with its engines off, far from all stars
A car turning round a bend at a constant speed
x: A car turning a bend changes the direction of its velocity, so it has centripetal acceleration and is non-inertial. Constant speed is the trap: the speed is constant but the velocity is not.

q: The second postulate of the special theory of relativity states that:
o: the speed of light depends on the speed of the source
the laws of physics are different in different inertial frames
the mass of a body is the same in all frames
the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers, whatever the motion of the source
x: Einstein's second postulate: light in a vacuum has the same speed c for every inertial observer, independent of the motion of the source or observer. The first postulate (same laws in all inertial frames) is often confused with it.

q: A spaceship moving towards the Earth at 0.6c switches on a forward-pointing lamp. What speed does an observer on the Earth measure for this light?
x: By the second postulate the speed of light is c for every inertial observer, whatever the motion of the source. Adding speeds the Galilean way gives the tempting but wrong 1.6c.

q: A closed laboratory moves at a constant velocity with no windows. Which statement about experiments done inside it is correct?
o: A pendulum's period becomes shorter in the direction of motion
No mechanical or optical experiment inside can show that the laboratory is moving
Light travels more slowly towards the front of the laboratory
A dropped ball falls towards the back of the laboratory
x: By the first postulate the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame, so no experiment inside can detect uniform motion. Light slowing towards the front is the tempting classical idea, but light has speed c in every inertial frame.

q: Inside a van accelerating forward at 2 m s⁻², a 5 kg box is observed from the van's frame. To explain its motion, the observer in the van must add a fictitious force of:
o: 10 N, opposite to the van's acceleration
10 N, in the direction of the van's acceleration
2.5 N, opposite to the van's acceleration
50 N, opposite to the van's acceleration
x: In a frame accelerating at a the fictitious force is ma = 5 × 2 = 10 N, directed opposite to the frame's acceleration (the box seems pushed backwards). Taking the direction along the acceleration is the common slip.

q: A clock on a spaceship moving at 0.6c relative to the Earth records an interval of 4 s. What interval does an observer on the Earth measure for the same two ticks?
x: √(1 − v²/c²) = √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8, so t = t₀/0.8 = 4/0.8 = 5 s (moving clocks run slow, so the Earth interval is longer). Multiplying by 0.8 instead gives 3.2 s.

q: A rod has a length of 10 m when at rest. What length does an observer measure when the rod moves along its length at 0.8c?
x: L = L₀√(1 − v²/c²) = 10 × √(1 − 0.64) = 10 × 0.6 = 6 m. Forgetting the square root gives 10 × 0.36 = 3.6 m; dividing instead of multiplying gives 16.7 m.

q: A metre stick moves at 0.8c in a direction perpendicular to its length. What length does a stationary observer measure for it?
x: Length contraction happens only along the direction of motion, so a length perpendicular to the velocity is unchanged: 1 m. Applying the factor 0.6 anyway gives the tempting 0.6 m.

q: A body has a rest mass of 2 kg. What is its relativistic mass when it moves at 0.6c?
x: m = m₀/√(1 − v²/c²) = 2/0.8 = 2.5 kg. Multiplying by 0.8 gives 1.6 kg; dividing by 0.64 (forgetting the square root) gives 3.125 kg.

q: An unstable particle has a lifetime of 3 μs in its own rest frame and moves at 0.8c through a laboratory. How far does it travel in the laboratory during one lifetime? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: √(1 − 0.64) = 0.6, so the lab lifetime is 3/0.6 = 5 μs; distance = 0.8 × 3 × 10⁸ × 5 × 10⁻⁶ = 1200 m. Ignoring time dilation gives 2.4 × 10⁸ × 3 × 10⁻⁶ = 720 m.

q: Two lamps at opposite ends of a long platform flash at the same instant for an observer standing on the platform. For an observer in a train moving fast along the platform, the two flashes are:
o: simultaneous only if the train moves faster than light
seen as a single flash at one place
x: Simultaneity is relative: events at different places that are simultaneous in one frame are not simultaneous in a frame moving along the line joining them. Assuming absolute time, as in Newtonian physics, gives the tempting 'simultaneous for every observer'.

q: At what speed must a rod move along its length for its measured length to be half its rest length?
x: √(1 − v²/c²) = ½ gives 1 − v²/c² = ¼, so v²/c² = ¾ and v = (√3/2)c ≈ 0.87c. Taking v²/c² = ¾ as the speed itself gives 0.75c.

q: A clock moves at a speed at which its relativistic mass is 25% greater than its rest mass. An interval of 60 min on this clock is measured by a stationary observer as:
x: m = 1.25m₀ means 1/√(1 − v²/c²) = 1.25, and the same factor stretches time: t = 1.25 × 60 = 75 min. Dividing by 1.25 gives 48 min; using 1.25² gives 93.75 min.

q: What is the energy equivalent of a mass of 2 kg? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: E = mc² = 2 × (3 × 10⁸)² = 2 × 9 × 10¹⁶ = 1.8 × 10¹⁷ J. Forgetting to square c gives 6 × 10⁸ J.

q: How much energy is equivalent to a mass of 1 g? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: m = 1 g = 10⁻³ kg, so E = mc² = 10⁻³ × 9 × 10¹⁶ = 9 × 10¹³ J. Leaving the mass as 1 (not converting grams to kilograms) gives 9 × 10¹⁶ J.

q: In a nuclear reaction 9 × 10¹⁰ J of energy is released. How much mass is converted into energy? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: m = E/c² = 9 × 10¹⁰/(9 × 10¹⁶) = 1 × 10⁻⁶ kg (1 mg). Dividing by c instead of c² gives 3 × 10² kg.

q: What is the rest mass energy of an electron? (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: E₀ = mₑc² = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 9 × 10¹⁶ = 81.9 × 10⁻¹⁵ ≈ 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J (about 0.51 MeV). Forgetting to square c gives 2.7 × 10⁻²² J.

q: A particle of rest mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg moves at 0.6c. What is its relativistic kinetic energy? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: At 0.6c, m = m₀/0.8 = 1.25m₀, so K = (m − m₀)c² = 0.25 × 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ × 9 × 10¹⁶ = 3.6 × 10⁻¹¹ J. The classical ½m₀v² gives about 2.6 × 10⁻¹¹ J, and mc² = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ J is the total energy, not the kinetic energy.

q: A star radiates energy at a steady rate of 3.6 × 10²⁶ W. How much mass does it lose in one minute? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: Energy in 60 s = 3.6 × 10²⁶ × 60 = 2.16 × 10²⁸ J; m = E/c² = 2.16 × 10²⁸/(9 × 10¹⁶) = 2.4 × 10¹¹ kg. Forgetting the 60 s gives the per-second loss, 4 × 10⁹ kg.
